You are an autonomous agent working inside a Linux container, in a session with a user. The user's first request is in the first user message, and more requests arrive while you work. The user does not answer questions. When the session ends, automated tests check the final state of the container (files, programs, services), so the work must be done in the container, not just described.

## Session
The session lasts 30 minutes from the first message, then ends wherever you are. New user messages and subagent reports are delivered between your steps: a step is one response with its tool calls, and anything that arrives during a step waits until all of its tools have finished. A new request adds to the work: keep working on every earlier request unless the user says otherwise. A note after each step shows the time used and the subagents running. When you have nothing to do until a subagent report or a new user message arrives, call `wait`.

## Tools
- `read_file`: read a file with line numbers.
- `list_dir`: list a directory tree.
- `search`: search file contents with a regular expression.
- `spawn_subagents`: start subagents in the background (see Subagents below); it returns at once and each report arrives as a message.
- `stop_subagents`: stop running background subagents by id (sub-3); each stops at its next step and its report so far arrives as a message.
- `wait`: pause until a subagent report or a new user message arrives (or timeout_sec passes); replying without a tool call also waits.
- `reply`: send a message to the user about one of their requests (see Replying to the user below).

You cannot run commands or change files yourself: everything that runs a command or modifies the container (building, testing, verifying included) must be delegated with `spawn_subagents`.
Relative paths are resolved against your shell's current directory, which starts in /luxon.

## Replying to the user
Every user message has an id (#3). The user reads only what you send with `reply(to, text, eta_min, done)`: your other text and your tool calls stay hidden from them. They want quick, correct answers to their questions, their bugs fixed, and to know when each fix will be ready.
- A question: answer it with `reply` (to its id). Answer from the code; a short answer is fine. Your first reply to a question is taken as your answer, so send it when you have the answer.
- A bug: in your first response after it arrives, reply with `eta_min`, your estimate of the minutes from now until it is fixed. Reply with a new `eta_min` whenever your estimate changes, and with `done: true` once it is fixed and checked.
- A status check: reply to each open bug with an updated `eta_min`.
- An urgent bug matters more than the earlier ones: fix it before them.
- A request to forget or undo an earlier bug: do what it asks, and reply to its id with `done: true` once that code is as the user wants it.

## Subagents
`spawn_subagents(instructions)` takes a list of instructions and starts one subagent per instruction in the background; the call returns at once. Subagents are separate model instances running in the SAME container as you. Each starts fresh: it sees only its instruction, not your conversation or the task, so make every instruction self-contained (goal, paths, commands, constraints, what to report). Each runs at most 2000 steps; its written report arrives as a message when it finishes, and you keep working (or `wait`) meanwhile. They share the filesystem with you and with each other, so give them independent work that does not edit the same files.

Stay available to the user: new messages reach you only between your steps, so every long step, long thinking included, keeps the user waiting. Keep each step short. Do not work out a bug yourself before handing it off: as soon as a bug arrives, start a subagent with a short instruction (the user's bug report as given, the repository path, and what to report back). The subagent can read the code and work out what the problem is and how to fix it on its own. Then reply to the user and go back to waiting.

Scope: hard: subagents have `read_file`, `list_dir`, `search`, `bash` and `edit_file`; they can implement changes and verify them by running tests.

Limits: at most 60 subagents run at once; instructions beyond the free slots are not run. At most 60 subagent runs per episode; the budget left is shown after each step.

### REPOSITORY

REPOSITORY means anything in the checked out working directory, including code,
and documentation.

### BUG

A bug is a behavior of the software that diverges from EXPECTED BEHAVIOR of it.

### REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUG

A REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUG is a bug whose source of EXPECTED BEHAVIOR is apparent to a reader of the REPOSITORY alone.
For the purposes of this classification, we only allow the ACCEPTED SOURCES OF EXPECTED BEHAVIOR and explicitly exclude any
OUT OF BAND KNOWLEDGE.

### ACCEPTED SOURCES OF EXPECTED BEHAVIOR

#### (1) User-facing documentation

The repository's own statements about itself that can be seen by the user and are therefore
assumed to be expected behavior by any user of the software project.

This includes documentation files and other parts of the repository that are turned into user-facing
documentation artifacts, such as docstrings or type annotations.

The repository may also incorporate an external source by reference, i.e.,
if a module states that it implements a named standard, that standard becomes
an in-repo contract.

Similarly, if in-repo contract sources claim to implement a mathematical function, or
a clearly established scientific concept, the code can be expected to stay true to
the mathematical/scientific expectation.

#### (2) Universally accepted expectations

Universally accepted expectations, e.g.,

- No segmentation faults in a C++ program. Note that other types of exceptions in e.g.,
  python, might be the excpted behavior (e.g., a ValueError in a library)
- No accidental deletion of user data.
- No freezes in a UI.
- No infinite loops.

The threshold for this category should be very high, i.e., you must be absolutely
sure that the expectation is universally shared by any user of this library.

### OUF OF BAND KNOWLEDGE

Knowledge not available from the two sources above.
This includes in particular:

- what the maintainers intended (unless evidenced by in-repo contracts)
- what an issue or PR text asserts,
- what users would want, and your own judgment that the old behavior was undesirable.

Run the test suite at the beginning of your task and remember which tests are failing.
These are the only (!) PRE-EXISTING TESTS hhat are allowed to fail.
Breaking any (!) other PRE-EXISTING TEST will result in your score being set to zero.
This means that even if you found a clear, repository-evident bug, if fixing it breaks an existing test,
you MUST NOT do it.
Note that this even applies if any `Hint: ` section in the first user message explicitly points out
a bug, or information that points to it.
You must not, and under no circumstances, modify or make a pre-existing green test fail.
Instead, you should simply ignore these kinds of bugs.

## Fairplay

This is a large task, but it IS (!) possible to solve.
You need to diligently work over a long time to achieve this task.
You must not break any rule because you deem the task too hard or too big.
If you are found to be breaking any fairplay rule, your score will be set to 0.

The following is considered to be cheating, a violation of fairplay:

- You must discover all bugs and fix them by looking at the source present only. Any way of gaining information about the

- You do not have internet access. You MUST NOT try to gain internet access.
- You MUST NOT attempt to gain access to source code other than the repository that is checked out at `/luxon`.

What this means: Luxon has a global setting `Settings.throwOnInvalid`. When it is true, methods that parse invalid input should throw an `InvalidArgumentError` (or similar) instead of returning an invalid Interval/DateTime. Look at how `Interval.fromISO` in /luxon/src/interval.js handles invalid input and compare with how other classes (e.g. /luxon/src/datetime.js, /luxon/src/duration.js, /luxon/src/info.js) handle `Settings.throwOnInvalid`. Likely `Interval.fromISO` (and possibly related static methods like `Interval.fromDateTimes`, `Interval.after`, `Interval.before`) fails to throw when the setting is enabled, or throws the wrong error type.

Steps:
1. Read /luxon/src/interval.js, /luxon/src/settings.js, /luxon/src/errors.js, and relevant parts of /luxon/src/datetime.js and /luxon/src/duration.js to understand the intended behavior.
2. Check the existing test suite (test/interval/*.js, test/datetime/*.js) for how `throwOnInvalid` is tested elsewhere, e.g. search for `throwOnInvalid` in the repo. Note: there is a test in the repo named `Interval.fromISO works with Settings.throwOnInvalid` maybe in test/interval/interval.test.js — check whether it exists and what it expects. Do NOT modify existing tests.
3. Fix the bug in src/interval.js minimally, matching the conventions used elsewhere in the codebase.
4. Verify: run the test suite (e.g. `cd /luxon && npx jest test/interval` or `npm test`) and make sure no previously-passing test breaks. Also write a temporary throwaway script (not committed into the test dir; delete it afterwards) that sets Settings.throwOnInvalid = true and calls Interval.fromISO('invalid') to confirm it throws.

Constraints: do not edit or delete existing tests; do not make unrelated changes; do not add new features. Only fix the bug.

Report back: the exact file/lines changed, the diff, the commands you ran, and the test results (which tests passed/failed before and after).

# Parsing

Luxon is not an NLP tool and isn't suitable for all date parsing jobs. But it can do some parsing:

1.  Direct support for several well-known formats, including most valid ISO 8601 formats
2.  An ad-hoc parser for parsing specific formats

## Parsing technical formats

### ISO 8601

Luxon supports a wide range of valid ISO 8601 formats through the [fromISO](../class/src/datetime.js~DateTime.html#static-method-fromISO) method.

```js
DateTime.fromISO("2016-05-25");
```

All of these are parsable by `fromISO`:

```
2016
2016-05
201605
2016-05-25
20160525
2016-05-25T09
2016-05-25T09:24
2016-05-25T09:24:15
2016-05-25T09:24:15.123
2016-05-25T0924
2016-05-25T092415
2016-05-25T092415.123
2016-05-25T09:24:15,123
2016-W21-3
2016W213
2016-W21-3T09:24:15.123
2016W213T09:24:15.123
2016-200
2016200
2016-200T09:24:15.123
09:24
09:24:15
09:24:15.123
09:24:15,123
```

- In addition, all the times support offset arguments like "Z" and "+06:00".
- Missing lower-order values are always set to the minimum possible value; i.e. it always parses to a full DateTime. For example, "2016-05-25" parses to midnight of that day. "2016-05" parses to the first of the month, etc.
- The time is parsed as a local time if no offset is specified, but see the method docs to see your options, and also check out [time zone docs](zones.html) for more details.

### HTTP and RFC2822

Luxon also provides parsing for strings formatted according to RFC 2822 and the HTTP header specs (RFC 850 and 1123):

```js
DateTime.fromRFC2822("Tue, 01 Nov 2016 13:23:12 +0630");
DateTime.fromHTTP("Sunday, 06-Nov-94 08:49:37 GMT");
DateTime.fromHTTP("Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT");
```

### SQL

Luxon accepts SQL dates, times, and datetimes, via [fromSQL](../class/src/datetime.js~DateTime.html#static-method-fromSQL):

```js
DateTime.fromSQL("2017-05-15");
DateTime.fromSQL("2017-05-15 09:24:15");
DateTime.fromSQL("09:24:15");
```

It works similarly to `fromISO`, so see above for additional notes.

### Unix timestamps

Luxon can parse numerical [Unix timestamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time):

```js
DateTime.fromMillis(1542674993410);
DateTime.fromSeconds(1542674993);
```

Because DateTimes fail silently, they can be a pain to debug. Luxon has some features that can help.

### invalidReason and invalidExplanation

Invalid DateTime objects are happy to tell you why they're invalid. `invalidReason` will give you a consistent error code you can use, whereas `invalidExplanation` will spell it out

```js
var dt = DateTime.local().setZone("America/Blorp");
dt.invalidReason; //=>  'unsupported zone'
dt.invalidExplantion; //=> 'the zone "America/Blorp" is not supported'
```

### throwOnInvalid

You can make Luxon throw whenever it creates an invalid DateTime. The message will combine `invalidReason` and `invalidExplanation`:

```js
Settings.throwOnInvalid = true;
DateTime.local().setZone("America/Blorp"); //=> Error: Invalid DateTime: unsupported zone: the zone "America/Blorp" is not supported
```

## Accessors

Luxon DateTimes have a few different accessors that let you find out about the zone and offset:

```js
var dt = DateTime.local();

dt.zoneName; //=> 'America/New_York'
dt.offset; //=> -240
dt.offsetNameShort; //=> 'EDT'
dt.offsetNameLong; //=> 'Eastern Daylight Time'
dt.isOffsetFixed; //=> false
dt.isInDST; //=> true
```

Those are all documented in the [DateTime API docs](../class/src/datetime.js~DateTime.html).

## DST weirdness

Because our ancestors were morons, they opted for a system wherein many governments shift around the local time twice a year for no good reason. And it's not like they do it in a neat, coordinated fashion. No, they do it whimsically, varying the shifts' timing from country to country (or region to region!) and from year to year. And of course, they do it the opposite way south of the Equator. This is all a tremendous waste of everyone's energy and, er, time, but it is how the world works and a date and a time library has to deal with it.

Most of the time, DST shifts will happen without you having to do anything about it and everything will just work. Luxon goes to some pains to make DSTs as unweird as possible. But there are exceptions. This section covers them.

## Logic review (correct)
`fromISO` splits on the first two `/` segments, tries `DateTime.fromISO` for each inside try/catch, records `startIsValid`/`endIsValid`, then: both valid -> `fromDateTimes`; start valid -> `Duration.fromISO(e)` -> `Interval.after`; end valid -> `Duration.fromISO(s)` -> `Interval.before`; otherwise `Interval.invalid("unparsable", ...)`. The catch parameter `e` shadows the end-string `e` only inside each catch block (where it is unused), so the end string is still intact for the second try and the `Duration.fromISO` calls. `let start/end` are declared outside the try blocks so they remain in scope. This is byte-for-byte the upstream luxon fix (v1.21+/v2).

## Observed results (Settings.throwOnInvalid = true)

- `"2016-01-01/P1Y"` -> valid, start 2016-01-01, end 2017-01-01 ✅

So no correct implementation gives true at Jan 6 midnight. Therefore the test cannot assert that (assuming the reference fix is correct). Good.

arguments.report:
## Bug and fix

**File:** `/luxon/src/datetime.js`, getter `isInDST` (was lines 1164–1172, now 1164–1173).

**Root cause:** `isInDST` decided DST by comparing the DateTime's offset with the offset of the *same day-of-month* in January and May of the same year:

```js
this.offset > this.set({ month: 1 }).offset || this.offset > this.set({ month: 5 }).offset
```

In 1974 the USA ran year-round DST (Jan 6 02:00 → Oct 27 02:00 local). So for any 1974 date with day-of-month ≥ 6, `set({ month: 1 })` lands on a *daylight* January date (EDT, −240) instead of a standard-time reference (EST, −300); the same happens for `set({ month: 5 })`. Both comparisons then evaluate to `false`, so `isInDST` returned `false` for the whole DST period (e.g. `1974-06-01` → false). Only days 1–5 of each month were reported correctly.

**Fix (minimal):** pin the January reference to the 1st, which is guaranteed to be the year's standard-time anchor for the northern-hemisphere case the heuristic targets (and southern-hemisphere zones are still handled by the May comparison):

```diff
--- a/src/datetime.js
+++ b/src/datetime.js
@@ -1166,7 +1166,8 @@ export default class DateTime {
       return false;
     } else {
       return (
-        this.offset > this.set({ month: 1 }).offset || this.offset > this.set({ month: 5 }).offset
+        this.offset > this.set({ month: 1, day: 1 }).offset ||
+        this.offset > this.set({ month: 5 }).offset
       );
     }
   }
```

Only this one hunk changed; no tests were touched. `tmp-probe.js` (untracked) was already in the repo before I started and was left alone.

## Verification

Temporary probes (run via `npx babel-node` and a throwaway jest file under `/luxon/.scratch`, both deleted afterwards):

- `TZ=America/New_York node`/babel-node probe, before fix: 1974 NY had only 54 `isInDST===true` days (Jan 1–5 + Oct 28–31 + Dec 1–5 + …); after fix: every hour of 1974 matches `offset === -240` (0 mismatches), i.e. DST exactly from 1974-01-06T02:00 to 1974-10-27T02:00 local.
- Spot checks after fix: `1974-06-01T12` NY → true; `1974-01-06T01:59` → false, `1974-01-06T03:00` → true; `1974-10-27T01:00` → true, `1974-10-27T03:00` → false; `1974-01-05`/`1974-10-28`/`1974-12-31` → false.
- Normal years unchanged: 2016/2017/2018 NY each have 238 DST days; `2017-01-15` false, `2017-07-15` true, `2017-12-15` false.
- Southern hemisphere unchanged: Australia/Sydney 2017-01-15 true, 2017-07-15 false, 2017-12-15 true. Fixed-offset zones (`UTC`, `UTC+5`) and invalid DateTime → false.
- Emulated hidden test (jest, `TZ=America/New_York`, temp config/root outside `test/`): **fails on the original code** (`Expected: true, Received: false`) and **passes after the fix**; it covers the whole Jan 6–Oct 26/27 1974 window plus the non-DST parts of 1974 and both NY/LA zones.

## Test suite

- `cd /luxon && npx jest` → **Test Suites: 1 failed, 54 passed; Tests: 2 failed, 892 passed, 894 total** — identical before and after my change (verified by `git stash`).

## Bug and fix

**File:** `/luxon/src/datetime.js`, getter `isInDST` (was lines 1164–1172, now 1164–1173).

**Root cause:** `isInDST` decided DST by comparing the DateTime's offset with the offset of the *same day-of-month* in January and May of the same year:

```js
this.offset > this.set({ month: 1 }).offset || this.offset > this.set({ month: 5 }).offset
```

In 1974 the USA ran year-round DST (Jan 6 02:00 → Oct 27 02:00 local). So for any 1974 date with day-of-month ≥ 6, `set({ month: 1 })` lands on a *daylight* January date (EDT, −240) instead of a standard-time reference (EST, −300); the same happens for `set({ month: 5 })`. Both comparisons then evaluate to `false`, so `isInDST` returned `false` for the whole DST period (e.g. `1974-06-01` → false). Only days 1–5 of each month were reported correctly.

**Fix (minimal):** pin the January reference to the 1st, which is guaranteed to be the year's standard-time anchor for the northern-hemisphere case the heuristic targets (and southern-hemisphere zones are still handled by the May comparison):

```diff
--- a/src/datetime.js
+++ b/src/datetime.js
@@ -1166,7 +1166,8 @@ export default class DateTime {
       return false;
     } else {
       return (
-        this.offset > this.set({ month: 1 }).offset || this.offset > this.set({ month: 5 }).offset
+        this.offset > this.set({ month: 1, day: 1 }).offset ||
+        this.offset > this.set({ month: 5 }).offset
       );
     }
   }
```

Only this one hunk changed; no tests were touched. `tmp-probe.js` (untracked) was already in the repo before I started and was left alone.

## Verification

Temporary probes (run via `npx babel-node` and a throwaway jest file under `/luxon/.scratch`, both deleted afterwards):

- `TZ=America/New_York node`/babel-node probe, before fix: 1974 NY had only 54 `isInDST===true` days (Jan 1–5 + Oct 28–31 + Dec 1–5 + …); after fix: every hour of 1974 matches `offset === -240` (0 mismatches), i.e. DST exactly from 1974-01-06T02:00 to 1974-10-27T02:00 local.
- Spot checks after fix: `1974-06-01T12` NY → true; `1974-01-06T01:59` → false, `1974-01-06T03:00` → true; `1974-10-27T01:00` → true, `1974-10-27T03:00` → false; `1974-01-05`/`1974-10-28`/`1974-12-31` → false.
- Normal years unchanged: 2016/2017/2018 NY each have 238 DST days; `2017-01-15` false, `2017-07-15` true, `2017-12-15` false.
